title: New Orleans pralines
subtitle: creamy pecan patties beaten to a grainy, fudgy set
excerpt: New Orleans pralines are not the hard, glassy nut-brittle pralines of French confectionery but something altogether softer: flat, creamy patties of butter-enriched sugar beaten with whole pecans until the mixture grains and sets to a crumbly, fudgy disc. They are made by cooking brown sugar and cream to soft-ball stage, adding pecans, and then beating off the heat until the gloss disappears and the mixture thickens enough to drop into rounds.
sourceNotes: New Orleans pralines are a distinct American confection with Creole roots, descended from the French sugar-coated almonds brought by French settlers in the 18th century. The shift from almonds to pecans (native to the region) and the addition of cream to produce a soft, grainy texture rather than a hard candy are the defining American adaptations. The confection has been made in New Orleans since at least the early 19th century and is documented in Creole cookery books from the 1900s onward.

recipe.batchNotes: Praline sugar does not scale reliably in a larger batch; the heat distribution and beating changes. Make consecutive batches instead.

glossaryTerms.definition: The sugar cooking stage reached at 112 to 116°C, where a small amount of syrup dropped into cold water forms a soft, pliable ball that flattens when removed. This is the target temperature for fudge, pralines, and similar grainy confections.

content.text: Line two baking trays with baking paper. Have a tablespoon and a wooden spoon ready. Once the sugar reaches temperature and the beating starts, you have about 3 to 4 minutes to drop the pralines before the mixture sets in the pan.

Combine {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{caster-sugar}}, and {{double-cream}} in a heavy-based saucepan over a medium heat. Stir until the sugars dissolve, then stop stirring and clip on a thermometer. Bring to soft-ball stage, 115°C, without stirring. The mixture will bubble actively; keep the heat steady. At 115°C, remove from the heat and add {{unsalted-butter}}, {{sea-salt-fine}}, and {{vanilla-extract}} without stirring. Leave undisturbed for 2 minutes.

Add the chopped {{pecans}} to the pan. Beat the mixture vigorously with a wooden spoon in a circular motion. As you beat, the mixture will lighten in colour, lose its gloss, and begin to thicken to a fudge-like consistency. This takes 2 to 3 minutes of constant beating. Stop when the mixture is thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon but still just fluid enough to pour. Do not overbeat: if it sets solid in the pan, return briefly to very low heat with a splash of cream and stir quickly.

Working quickly, drop heaped tablespoons of the mixture onto the lined trays, spacing them about 4 cm apart to allow for slight spreading. Press a pecan half into the centre of each one. The pralines will spread slightly into rough rounds. Leave undisturbed at room temperature for 25 to 30 minutes until completely firm and no longer tacky to the touch. Do not move them before they have fully set.
